drills.coachNote: The knight on c6 is only defended once, by the bishop on d7 — and your bishop on e4 is already aimed straight at it. Bxc6 wins material cleanly: after Bxc6 Bxc6 Qxc6, your queen doesn't just take the bishop, it lands on c6 forking the rook on a8 along the empty b7-diagonal. Kh2 walks right past that, so instead Black grabs a free tempo with Bg4, hitting your queen on f3, and you hand back most of the edge you'd earned. Before playing a quiet move, count attackers versus defenders on any piece sitting in your crosshairs.

Grabbing the pawn with Qxh5 feels free, but it lets Black off the hook — Rh8 swings the rook onto the newly-opened h-file straight at your king and queen, forcing Qf3 and giving up the initiative you'd built. A free pawn on the rim is never worth more than a piece sitting one capture away.

drills.coachNote: You're so far up here that the pawn on a2 is basically a free queen — nothing stops a1=Q, and even if the knight on b3 hops back to a1 and grabs it, you're still completely winning and can just tuck the king with Kh7. Rg4+ throws that away on a check that accomplishes nothing: no material, no mate threat, and it lets White's king calmly walk to f2 and then scoop your e2 pawn with Rxe2 before your knight can guard it. When you're this far ahead, stop hunting for checks and play the move that simplifies — promote the pawn or tidy up the king.

Rf1 lets go of the pin: the knight is no longer tied down, so it jumps in with Nxe2 and grabs your pawn, and you have to scramble to win material back with Rd8+ and a fork on d1. You still come out ahead because you were already so far up, but Rd8 was the clean way to cash in the pin instead of the messy one.

drills.title: vs Racheeeedgr (827) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Qc4+ was coming no matter what you played — it's along the c4-g8 diagonal, and g6 doesn't block that, it only takes away g7 as an escape square for your own king. So White gets the check for free, you're forced into Kh7, and then g4 starts rolling a pawn storm toward your king while your queen sits passively on h5. Qb5 was the better use of that move — it puts your queen on an active square pressuring White's queen and prepares to simplify into a winning endgame, with Kg2 Kf8 Kf2 Qd7 showing you calmly centralizing your king instead. In queen endings every tempo matters — spend it improving your worst-placed piece, not on a pawn move that stops nothing.

drills.coachNote: The knight looked like a nice centralizing jump, but e4 is exactly the square White's queen can hit with a check first — Qf5+ lands on the f5-h7 diagonal against your king on h7, and only after you're forced into Kh8 does Qxe4 come and win the knight for nothing. That's the pattern to watch for: a check before the capture, so material disappears in an in-between move you didn't see coming. Qe8 was the fix — it keeps the knight safely covering f6 and brings your queen into the game, and after Qc2+ Kh8 Qc4 Qe1 you're the one generating threats instead of losing a piece to one. Before advancing a piece, check whether the enemy queen has a checking square that lands on it first.

Qxb7 won a bishop but allowed Qd5 — a queen trade you can't decline (Qxd5 exd5) — and with queens off, the attack on f6 vanished, about five pawns of advantage.

drills.coachNote: You had a mating attack going — Black's king is stuck out on f6 — and stopping to grab the loose bishop on b7 is exactly the wrong moment to pause. Qxb7 lets Black play Qd5, offering a trade that leads to Qxd5 exd5, and your crushing +8 attack gets simplified down into a merely-winning endgame — you traded a mating attack for one extra piece. Ne5 kept the hunt alive instead: it heads for d7+, checking the king again and driving it to g5, walking further into trouble. When the enemy king is this exposed, keep generating checks and threats before you stop to collect material — the attack is worth more than any single piece.

drills.explanation: Ne5 puts the knight on a square the d4 pawn protects and attacks the knight on g6. If Nxe5, dxe5+ regains the piece with check, and after Qxe5 your Qf3+ keeps queens on against his airy king. Your Qf3+ instead offered the trade Black wanted: Qxf3 gxf3 killed all the pressure, and Nf4 came next, poking at the h3 pawn.
drills.title: vs sudharsanee (850) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Variation
drills.coachNote: Same idea as the last mistake — Black's king is still stuck on f6, and Qf3+ rushes straight into a trade: Qxf3, gxf3, and your mating attack collapses into a plain endgame where you're only clearly better instead of completely winning. Ne5 keeps squeezing instead — it offers the knight, and after Nxe5 dxe5+ your pawn recaptures with check, because the king is still on f6, winning a free tempo. Only then does Qf3+ actually land with force, driving the king to g7 after you've gained more ground first. Ask whether a quieter move can set up a bigger version of the check you're about to play, instead of cashing it in immediately.

drills.explanation: Both your queen and rook could capture the knight on f4, but Qxf4 is the right way: it wins the knight while the rook on f8 keeps guarding its partner on e8. Rxf4 abandoned that rook — Qxe8+ snapped it off with check, and after Kh7, Qe6 left White completely consolidated. Taking with the wrong piece cost about six pawns.
drills.title: vs prusten63 (873) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Check what your rook on f8 is doing before you move it — it's the only piece guarding your other rook on e8, since they sit right next to each other on the back rank. Rxf4 pulls it away to grab the knight, and White answers Qxe8+, winning your other rook with check because nothing covers it anymore — after Kh7 Qe6 you've given back far more than you gained. Qxf4 wins the same knight safely: the queen takes it instead, your rook stays on f8, e8 stays covered, and the trades that follow stay clean. Before moving a rook off the back rank, always check what it was quietly guarding.

drills.explanation: a6 strikes at White's overextended queenside: after bxa6 Rxa6 your rook enters the game down the a-file, and b5 is met calmly by Ra8. Castling let White play Qe2, hitting your knight on c4 — a piece with no defenders — and you had to scramble with c6 and b5 just to hold it, leaving White a wedge pawn on c6.
drills.title: vs prusten63 (873) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Before you castle, look at your knight on c4 — nothing black actually defends it, it's just sitting there hoping White doesn't notice. Your rook on a8 and the b6/d6 pawns are begging you to play a6, hitting White's pawn on b5 right now. Instead O-O lets White play Qe2, lining the queen up on the open d1-c4 diagonal to hit that knight, and after ...c6 bxc6 your queenside structure gets ripped open while the knight's still stuck answering for itself — that's the 2.5 pawns you lose. a6 first (bxa6 Rxa6) gets your rook swinging to a6 and prepares ...b5 yourself, so you're setting the agenda instead of reacting to White's.

drills.explanation: You were a full piece up and just needed to consolidate. c5 gains space, and the knight calmly reroutes to c6 next with b6 and normal development to follow. Ng4 put the knight on a square covered by White's queen all the way back on d1 — Qxg4 took it for nothing, handing the extra piece straight back.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Look at the diagonal from White's queen on d1 to your knight on e5 — d1, e2, f3, g4 is completely open, nothing's on it. So the moment you play Ne5-g4, Qxg4 just wins the knight outright, no trick needed, before White even follows up with e5 and Qg3 to keep hounding your position. That's the whole story: a piece sitting on an open diagonal in front of the enemy queen, worth about three pawns gone for nothing. c5 was the move instead — it doesn't touch that diagonal at all, it just expands in the center, and after Re1 Nc6 b4 b6 Bb2 you're developing calmly with a fully sound position.

drills.explanation: Bxa2 trades off White's light-squared bishop on your terms: after Rxa2 you swing rooks to the e-file with Rae8 and Re6, sitting solidly behind the e5 pawn. Rad8 left the bishops eyeballing each other one move too long — Bh6 came with threats at your king, and after g6, Bxe6 fxe6 left you with doubled, weak e-pawns.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Look at your bishop on e6 — it's aiming straight down the long diagonal at White's bishop on a2, whose only defender is the rook on a1. Bxa2 just wins it: even after Rxa2 you're trading down material while massively ahead, and Rae8 next doubles rooks on the file where White's king lives. Rad8 skips that gift, and White gets to play Bh6, poking g7 and forcing ...g6, then Bxe6 fxe6 trades off your good bishop — 1.4 pawns of your winning edge given back for nothing. In a winning position, take the free piece before you build with the rest.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 wins a full rook: the knight captures its counterpart and forks the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so after Qd6 saves the queen, Nxd8 collects the rook and Qxg5 even adds a pawn. a4 instead gave Black time for Nxe5, trading off your monster knight, and after Qxe5 his other knight landed on e4 with real counterplay.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your knight on c5 has a shot right now: Nxc6 hits the knight there, and if Qd6 tries to trap it, your knight just jumps to d8 and eats the rook instead — Nxd8 Qxd8 wins you the exchange, then Qxg5 grabs a pawn on top. a4 skips all of that, and Black answers Nxe5, trading off your other strong knight; after Qxe5 Ne4 the black knight lands with tempo and your +4.8 evaluation collapses by 4.5 pawns almost instantly. With two knights that deep in enemy territory, hunt for the tactic they're threatening before spending a move on a slow pawn push.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 is a fork: from c6 the knight hits both the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so bxc6 is forced — wrecking the pawn cover in front of the king on c8. Then Qd3 turns on the knight on e4, and after Nxc5 bxc5 you're clearly on top. b5 abandoned the b4 pawn's guard of your c5 knight, and Nxe5 won material — no recapture worked.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Same idea you missed last move: Nxc6 wins material right now, and after bxc6 Qd3 you're simplifying into a clean, safe edge. Also notice your knight on e5 isn't actually protected — your queen sits on e3, but your own knight on e4 blocks the file, so nothing defends e5. b5 ignores both points, and Black plays Nxe5, picking the knight off for free while you're busy pushing queenside pawns with bxa6. That's how +1.2 turns into trouble in one move — before every pawn push, check whether your most advanced pieces are actually covered.

drills.explanation: Rxf7 forces mate in three: your queen on d5 X-rays g8 so f7 can't really be held, and after Rg7+ Kh8, Rg8 is checkmate — the bishop on f6 seals g7 while the queen on d5 guards g8, so the rook can't be taken. Qg5 instead let Black play Rxf2 and keep the counterplay alive.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: You had forced mate on the board: Rxf7 rips away Black's last defender, and after Re2 Rg7+ Kh8, Rg8 is checkmate. Qg5 lets that slip — it's not a terrible square, but it hands Black a free tempo to play Rxf2, and suddenly the queen and rook you've let sit on b2 and c2 are crashing into your own king's cover instead of you finishing the job. That single tempo is the whole 18-pawn swing — 'completely won' evaporating because the mate needed to start immediately, not after one more useful-looking move. When mate is on the board, calculate it fully before reaching for the safe-looking option.

drills.explanation: Qxc8 wins the rook on c8 outright — Black never dares recapture, since your bishop on f6 and rook on e7 strangle his king; he tries Qb5, and after Re8 he must throw his queen away with Qf1+ Rxf1. Qd5 let a won game slip: Qxa3, and after Qxd4, Qxh3 stripped your king — nearly fifteen pawns of advantage gone.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: Look at the c-file — your queen on c4 has a clear road straight to the rook on c8, nothing in between. Qxc8 just wins a full rook for nothing. Instead Qd5 lets Black's queen on b2 go to work: Qxa3, then once your queen grabs the d4 pawn, Qxh3 too, ripping pawns off right next to your own king while the free rook sits untouched. That's the 14.9-pawn swing — a whole rook was there for the taking and you reached for a centralizing move instead. Before improving a piece, scan every enemy piece sitting on an open file or diagonal from your queen first.

drills.explanation: The g5 pawn was attacking your bishop on f4, and Nxg5 meets that head-on — the knight is covered by that same bishop, and after fxg5 Bxg5 Black's kingside pawns are stripped while his pieces retreat to passive squares like Nf6 and Nb8 as Qf3 builds pressure. Bf5+ dropped a whole piece instead: e6 blocked the check and hit the bishop, and after Bc2, gxf4 won your dark-squared bishop.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your real target is Black's king stuck on d7 and that weak g5 pawn, which is only defended by the f6 pawn — Nxg5 rips right into it: fxg5 Bxg5 nets you pawns and a real attack on that exposed king. Bf5+ looks tempting because it's check, but it's the wrong kind of check — it lets Black answer ...e6, kicking your bishop back to c2 for nothing, and Black just consolidates while your attacking piece retreats empty-handed. You still drew the game, but you traded a real initiative against an uncastled king for one shot of 'check' that accomplished nothing — 3.3 pawns of advantage, gone. Ask what a check actually achieves before playing it.

drills.explanation: Nxg5 was the shot: after fxg5 Bxg5 you get two pawns for the knight and Black's king on d7 is stranded, with Qf3 coming to hit the loose d5 pawn (the simple e4 was strong too). Bf5+ backfired — e6 blocked with tempo, the bishop crawled back to c2, and gxf4 scooped up your dark-squared bishop, which the g5 pawn had been eyeing all along.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Before you go hunting for checks, look at what's undefended on your own side — your bishop on f4 has zero protection, and Black's pawn on g5 is sitting right on the diagonal that eats it. Bf5+ feels active, but it's just a spent tempo: Black plays e6, your bishop retreats to c2, and then gxf4 simply removes your other bishop for free — you've handed away a full piece for one check. The move was e4, striking the center instead of chasing checks; after gxf4 exd5 you're already grabbing the d5 pawn and hitting the knight on c6, real pressure instead of a giveaway. Rule of thumb: before any 'free' check, scan what you're leaving hanging.

drills.explanation: Your knight on e4 was attacked by the d3 pawn, and Nd6 is the safe retreat — White wins the e5 pawn with Rxe5+, but Be7 blocks, Bg6 follows, and you're only down a pawn with pieces coming out. Ng5 ran the knight straight onto the c1-bishop's diagonal: Bxg5 won it outright, and White grabbed e5 with the knight as well.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Scan every line pointing at a square before you land a piece there — White's bishop on c1 sits on the open c1-h6 diagonal with nothing in the way, so g5 was never safe. Bxg5 just wins your knight outright, and then f6, Nxe5 mops up the e5 pawn too while you're down a full piece for nothing. Nd6 kept the knight working instead, still eyeing that same f5-a5 diagonal, and after Rxe5+ Be7 Qe2 you're only down a pawn instead of a piece — a real game instead of a lost one. Check who's aiming at the square before you commit a piece to it.

drills.explanation: Your knight on g5 was attacked by the bishop on c1, defended only by your queen along the d8–g5 diagonal — and Be7 blocked that exact diagonal. Bxg5 won the knight, and after Be6, Bxe7 Qxe7 left White a clean piece up. Ne6 just steps to safety; after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the position stays a fair fight.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Your knight on g5 was already hanging from last move, and instead of rescuing it you developed with Be7 — that doesn't change anything about c1's diagonal. Bxg5 just takes the knight, and even though Be6, Bxe7, Qxe7 trades bishops afterward, you're still down the knight for nothing since that trade was even. Ne6 was the fix — pull the piece off the attacked square first, then after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the position is sharp but you're not just shedding material. When a piece is hanging, that's the move that has to happen before anything else on the board gets your attention.

drills.explanation: Bc7 hits the queen on d8 and grabs a square deep in Black's camp: after Qd7, b6 locks the bishop on c7 permanently, cramping the whole queenside while Ra4 swings the rook toward the action. Your e4 gave Black a free move for Bd7, developing with a hit on the b5 pawn — the same Bc7 idea then came a tempo late, and the queen slipped away to c8.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Black's queen on d8 is stuck behind an undeveloped bishop on c8, and Bc7 hits that queen directly while also eyeing b8 — it forces Qd7, and then b6 clamps the whole queenside shut with the bishop and rook on a8 struggling to get out, exactly what Ra4 and pressure down the a-file want to exploit. e4 is a perfectly normal-looking pawn push, but it costs you the moment: Black gets a free tempo to play Bd7, untangling before you ever get to execute Bc7. You were still winning either way, but that's most of a two-pawn advantage given back for nothing — when a piece like that bishop can jump into the enemy's undeveloped pieces with tempo, take it before helping your center.

drills.explanation: Qc5 does three jobs: it confronts the queen on b6, attacks the knight on e7, and keeps the b5 pawn defended. After Qd8, Bd6 piles onto e7, and Bxe7 Rxe7 leaves you in full control of the dark squares. Qc3 left b5 with no defender at all — Bd7 came immediately, and after your too-late Qc5, Bxb5 took the pawn for free.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: The b5 pawn isn't defended by your knight on b3 or your queen — nothing covers it — so the moment Black gets a free move, that pawn is a target. Qc3 doesn't address any of that; it just lets Black play Bd7, and now the bishop is staring straight at b5, so Bxb5 just wins the pawn clean. Qc5 was the sharper idea — offering the trade forces Qd8, and then Bd6 hits the rook on f8 and sets up Bxe7 next, winning material back with tempo instead of donating a pawn. Look at what's actually hanging on your side of the board before you spend a move improving your queen's square.

drills.explanation: Nf5+ is a fork: it checks the king on g3 and attacks the rook on g7 at the same time. After Kf4 you play Nxg7, winning the rook and flipping the game — roughly twelve pawns of swing. Nb7 instead walked into Rc7+, and after Kd8 the rook simply captured the knight on b7.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: Even in a position this lost, there's still a fork sitting on the board for you — your knight on d6 can jump to f5, giving check to the king on g3 while simultaneously attacking the rook on g7. That's Nf5+, and after Kf4 you just play Nxg7 and win the rook outright, turning a hopeless position into a real fight. Instead Nb7 wanders the knight to an undefended square, and Rc7+ forks your king and that same knight — Kd8, Rxb7, and it's just gone, sealing the loss for nothing. Before you move a piece defensively, always check whether it has a fork or check of its own to give first.
